content: Children who are not diagnosed or reported as having tuberculosis (TB) are often referred to as missing cases. In 2020, it was estimated that 226,000 children under the age of 15 died from TB. Modeling studies have shown that 80% of TB-related deaths occur in children under the age of 5, and 96% of children who die from TB did not receive treatment. The low detection rate of TB in young children is attributed to several factors. First, young children often have paucibacillary TB, meaning they excrete very few bacteria, making it difficult to detect using current bacteriological tests. Second, there is a lack of sensitive, point-of-care diagnostic tests. Third, collecting appropriate respiratory samples for bacteriological confirmation is challenging. Lastly, TB symptoms in children often overlap with those of other common childhood diseases, leading to misdiagnosis. Primary healthcare (PHC) facilities, where children often first seek care, frequently lack the awareness, resources, and capacity to diagnose and manage pediatric TB. This includes limitations in sample collection, access to bacteriological tests, chest X-rays (CXR), and the ability to make clinical diagnoses when bacteriological testing is unavailable or yields negative results. Additionally, pediatric TB services are often centralized at secondary or tertiary healthcare levels and are managed in a vertical, non-integrated manner. TB screening is not systematically incorporated into clinical algorithms for child health. The World Health Organization (WHO) has introduced two new recommendations for diagnosing TB in children and adolescents. These include the use of the Xpert Ultra assay on gastric aspirate and stool specimens for diagnosing pulmonary TB (PTB) and detecting rifampicin resistance, as well as the use of integrated treatment decision algorithms for PTB diagnosis in children. Prior to 2022, the Xpert Ultra assay was already recommended for use on nasopharyngeal aspirate (NPA) and sputum specimens. The 2022 recommendations expand the range of specimens that can be tested and align with WHO's existing recommendations for the Xpert MTB/RIF assay. The Xpert Ultra assay represents a significant advancement in TB diagnostics, particularly for detecting rifampicin resistance. It has a lower limit of detection compared to the Xpert MTB/RIF assay and includes a trace semi-quantitative category. The assay is strongly recommended as the initial diagnostic test for TB and rifampicin resistance in children under 15 years of age with signs and symptoms of PTB. It is preferred over smear microscopy, culture, and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the Xpert Ultra assay on gastric aspirate and stool specimens in children. For gastric aspirate, the sensitivity was 64% and specificity was 95% against a microbiological reference standard. For stool specimens, the sensitivity was 53% and specificity was 98%. However, sensitivity estimates were lower when compared to a composite reference standard. No studies evaluated the assay's accuracy for detecting rifampicin resistance using gastric aspirate or stool specimens. The WHO's Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized that all TB tests, including the microbiological reference standard, have suboptimal sensitivity in children due to the paucibacillary nature of TB in this age group. A positive test result reliably indicates TB disease, but a negative result does not exclude it. The GDG highlighted the importance of interpreting test results within the clinical context and not relying solely on a negative test to rule out TB. The GDG also discussed the feasibility and acceptability of implementing the Xpert Ultra assay on gastric aspirate and stool specimens. Gastric aspirate collection requires trained staff, fasting, and often hospitalization, making it less feasible at lower levels of the healthcare system. In contrast, stool specimens are non-invasive and more acceptable to children, caregivers, and healthcare workers. Stool testing was found to be cost-effective in certain settings, such as primary healthcare centers in Uganda, even at low TB prevalence levels. Subgroup analyses were conducted for children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), children living with HIV, and different age groups. However, data were limited, particularly for children under 1 year of age and those aged 1–4 years. The GDG concluded that the Xpert Ultra assay on gastric aspirate, stool, NPA, and sputum specimens can be used as the preferred initial test for diagnosing PTB in children across all pediatric comorbidities and age subgroups. Implementation of the Xpert Ultra assay requires ensuring the quality of specimen collection. Gastric aspirate collection is invasive and may not be feasible at lower healthcare levels, while stool specimen collection is more practical and widely acceptable. Training and resources are necessary to optimize the use of these diagnostic tools, particularly in resource-limited settings. This explanation provides a detailed, professional summary of the content, maintaining the technical and clinical nuances of the original text.
